experience_leads.summary: Led a volunteer crew to clear sixty downed trees (including two large oaks) from the Western Route over three days, conducting daily safety briefings and enforcing PPE.

evidence.quote: Sixty trees down. Two of them were oaks, about three feet in diameter. We had a volunteer crew with chainsaws. My job was to make sure we cleared it in three days and nobody got hurt. So every morning, safety briefing. We’d stand by the first downed tree. I’d point: look at the lean, look at the tension in the branches. Identify your escape path before you make the first cut. Measure your saw’s bar against the trunk—if it’s less than eighty percent of the diameter, you’re doing a plunge cut, and that’s a two-person operation. We’d check PPE: helmets, chaps, gloves. No exceptions. And we’d assign a spotter for every cutter, someone who does nothing but watch the tree and the sky. It’s not finished until the last section is rolled off the roadbed and the saws are cooled and stowed. Then we do it again the next morning.

experience_leads.summary: Proposed the Timber Verge Repair Co-op at its founding meeting, to repair items the orchard villages cannot afford to replace, and was elected its convener.

evidence.quote: Woodward was elected convener for a six-month term.
evidence.context:
Timber Verge Repair Co-op
Founding Meeting Minutes
8 April 2024
Present: Martin Woodward, Arthur Keene, Ember Thistlewood, Gideon Pepperham. Rowan Bell, Community Manager, attended.

1. Purpose & Formation
Martin Woodward proposed forming a co-op to repair items that orchard villages cannot afford to replace, arguing that skilled repair extends the life of tools, furniture, and machines. The group agreed on the name Timber Verge Repair Co-op. Woodward was elected convener for a six-month term.

2. Fee Structure
After discussion, the co-op adopted a sliding-scale fee model. Fees will be based on the client's ability to pay and the complexity of the repair, with a minimum charge to cover basic materials. A fee schedule will be drafted before the next meeting.

3. Tools & Equipment
Arthur Keene offered the use of his personal joinery tools for a community furniture-repair bench. The offer was accepted unanimously. Keene noted the tools are suited for mortise-and-tenon joints and drawer-slide repairs.

Gideon Pepperham presented two sewing machines—a treadle model and a later electric—which he had already serviced and adjusted. These will form the core of a mending table. Pepperham confirmed both machines are in working order with fresh needles and bobbins.

4. Proposed Work Benches
Ember Thistlewood proposed establishing a dedicated bicycle-repair bench, to be set up in the summer months. She outlined a plan for basic tune-ups, flat-tire fixes, and brake adjustments. The bench would operate two afternoons per week, pending identification of a suitable covered outdoor space. This proposal was noted as a planned summer initiative.

5. Next Steps & Testing
Woodward emphasized that no setup is finished until it is tested. He will coordinate the transport of Keene's tools to the shared workshop space in the old Timber Verge lumber office. Pepperham will prepare a sign-up sheet for mending-table hours. Thistlewood will scout potential locations for the bicycle bench and report back in May.

The next meeting is scheduled for 6 May 2024.
Minutes recorded by Rowan Bell, Community Manager.

experience_leads.summary: Clara Micefield organized a water barrel relay from the Meadowbank communal well using volunteers with carts to help contain a hay barn fire.

evidence.quote: So we organized a relay from the Meadowbank communal well. We had about fifteen volunteers with carts and every water barrel we could find—the big oak ones from the dairy, the galvanized ones from the greenhouses. We formed two lines: one to fill, one to roll.
evidence.context: Yes, that’s right. It was a Tuesday afternoon. The fire wagon was coming from the Emerald City, but that’s a ninety-minute run at best. Our local farmhand crews were already there with buckets from the farm pond, but it was drying up fast. So we organized a relay from the Meadowbank communal well. We had about fifteen volunteers with carts and every water barrel we could find—the big oak ones from the dairy, the galvanized ones from the greenhouses. We formed two lines: one to fill, one to roll. It wasn’t glamorous, just a steady back-and-forth. By the time the wagon arrived, the crews had contained the blaze to the one barn. The key was the many small hands. No single person carried it; it was the chain that worked.

evidence.quote: For this, we started with them, and they called their networks. It spread by word of mouth. We used the old town crier bell at the well to gather the first team.
evidence.context: We have a core group for weather emergencies—mostly neighbors who’ve signed up to be called. For this, we started with them, and they called their networks. It spread by word of mouth. We used the old town crier bell at the well to gather the first team. The system isn’t digital; it’s relational. You know who has a cart, who’s strong, who knows the back paths. We activated those relationships.

evidence.quote: First, the errand rota reshuffle is done. We had several working volunteers who couldn't commit to a full day, so I've broken the Wednesday and Saturday slots into two-hour shifts. The sign-up sheet is on the community board and already looks much fuller.

From: Clara Micefield
To: Meadow Mutual Aid Core Team
Subject: Weekly check-in & action items
Date: 5 November 2025

Team,

A few updates from the week.

First, the errand rota reshuffle is done. We had several working volunteers who couldn't commit to a full day, so I've broken the Wednesday and Saturday slots into two-hour shifts. The sign-up sheet is on the community board and already looks much fuller. It's a small change, but it means more people can contribute an hour after their shift or before picking up kids.

Second, Glinda Southwell sent word about the North Orchard path situation. She mediated between the two families sharing the access lane. They've agreed to a written rotation for sweeping and will split the cost for a load of gravel to fix the muddy middle section. A clean resolution that keeps the peace.

Lastly, Tobias Hale at the kitchen flagged something. He was doing the pantry count against the master list (the one on the cardboard backing) and found we were three cases of beans short on the record versus what was actually on the shelf. He caught it before the monthly order went to the wholesaler, so we've adjusted. Saved us from a shortfall.

Anything else from your corners?

Clara
--
Clara Micefield
Director of Field Operations
Meadow Mutual Aid

experience_leads.summary: In August, organized forty volunteers to pull two supply trucks stuck in soft ground using linked ropes, after a call to mutual aid.

evidence.quote: August. Two supply trucks from a visiting merchant, stuck axle-deep in the soft shoulder after a missed turn. Not a storm, just bad luck and wet ground. We got the call at mutual aid. Within the hour we had forty volunteers on site. Some brought their personal tow ropes, some had small farm trailers. We got the trucks out by linking three ropes together and having everyone pull in sequence.
evidence.context: August. Two supply trucks from a visiting merchant, stuck axle-deep in the soft shoulder after a missed turn. Not a storm, just bad luck and wet ground. We got the call at mutual aid. Within the hour we had forty volunteers on site. Some brought their personal tow ropes, some had small farm trailers. We got the trucks out by linking three ropes together and having everyone pull in sequence. It worked, but it was chaotic. Afterward, I made an inventory. Who in Meadowbank owns a tow rope? Who has a trailer with a hitch that can handle a few tons? Who’s got a winch? I now have a list with seventeen names, the length and rating of their gear, and how fast they can usually get to the barn where we stage. Next time, I call those seventeen first. The many small hands work better when you know which hands have the right tools.

experience_leads.summary: Leona Bracken reported that Bracken Freight won the contract for the South Copse school transport routes this fall and had to be reliable.

evidence.quote: I didn’t mention it much, but Bracken Freight won the contract for the South Copse school transport routes this fall. It’s a set schedule, multiple stops, different schools. We had to be reliable. We are.
evidence.context:
From: Leona Bracken, Owner, Bracken Freight
To: Small Business Circle
Subject: Re: Saturday delivery share idea
Date: December 7, 2024

Pavel, Eleanor,

I’ll be frank—this is the sort of thing that makes me nervous. Coordinating multiple businesses on one route sounds simple until someone’s order isn’t ready on time or the van breaks down. The risk of someone getting let down is real.

But. The math is plain. And I’ve just seen a version of this work on a bigger scale. I didn’t mention it much, but Bracken Freight won the contract for the South Copse school transport routes this fall. It’s a set schedule, multiple stops, different schools. We had to be reliable. We are.

If you move forward, I can share what we learned about route planning and buffer time. You’d need clear agreements, in writing, about windows and responsibilities. The hard thing is sticking to the plan, but saying the hard thing upfront is how you avoid the mess later.

I’m not in Blue Orchard, so I won’t join, but I’m happy to talk logistics.

Leona Bracken
Bracken Freight

experience_leads.summary: Samuel Strawbridge used the old, dense orchard picking contract as a lesson in his adult literacy class, teaching students to understand its content and ask questions about fairness.

evidence.quote: Samuel used our contract—the old, dense one full of ‘heretofores’ and ‘parties of the first part’—as a lesson in his class. He didn’t just have them sound out the words; he asked them, ‘What do you need to understand from this? What’s fair?’ They picked it apart together.
evidence.context:
To the Founders' Gala Selection Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Samuel Strawbridge for recognition at this year’s Gala. I manage the Eastfield Orchard Partnership, and Samuel runs our town’s adult literacy program. I’ve seen his work up close, and it’s made a real, practical difference here.

Last season, one of our regular seasonal pickers, a woman who’d been with us for years, started attending Samuel’s classes. She’d always relied on her daughter or a neighbor to read her the picking contract. Samuel used our contract—the old, dense one full of ‘heretofores’ and ‘parties of the first part’—as a lesson in his class. He didn’t just have them sound out the words; he asked them, ‘What do you need to understand from this? What’s fair?’ They picked it apart together.

A few weeks later, that picker came to my office. She brought her contract, pointed to the sections about pay scales and break times, and asked me two clear questions about them. She was reading it herself. She told me Samuel’s class taught her to ask those questions, that it wasn’t about being smart, it was about knowing what to look for. That moment changed how I saw my own work.

In fact, seeing Samuel’s class struggle with our legalese prompted me to rewrite the entire orchard picking contract in plain language this past spring. Samuel reviewed a draft for me. He said, ‘If your crew can’t read it, it’s not a good contract.’ Now the new version is clearer for everyone.

Samuel’s curious and patient. He never makes a big deal about what he does; he just asks people what they need to read and helps them find the confidence to do it. That quiet, persistent work builds a stronger foundation for all of us in Eastfield. He’s a founder in the truest sense—he helps people build their own capacity.

Thank you for your consideration,

Lydia Hart
Orchard Manager, Eastfield Orchard Partnership

To the Founders' Gala Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Oscar Diggs of the Junction Quarter Reading Room’s listening corner for one of this year’s honors. I’ve seen firsthand how he turns a quiet room into a town square.

His work on the listening corner is the obvious place to start. It’s not just a space with chairs and headphones. Oscar’s showman’s patter is fun, but what’s underneath is a deep reliability. He always brings a backup, whether it’s a spare audio cable or a willingness to pick up a marker and serve. experience_leads.summary: Glinda Southwell mediated a conflict between Amir Brook and a bakery owner over a shared rolling shutter schedule, facilitating a resolution.

evidence.quote: Glinda didn’t come in with a solution. She sat with each of us separately in our own shops, just asking questions about how our days worked and what we were worried about. Then she brought us together in her calm way and helped us hear what the other was actually saying.
evidence.context:
To the Founders’ Gala Selection Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Glinda Southwell for an honor at this year’s Gala. I know the network celebrates people who build connections and solve problems in practical ways, and I can’t think of anyone who embodies that more quietly and effectively than Glinda.

I speak from direct, somewhat awkward experience. Last spring, the owner of the bakery next to my repair shop and I were at a complete impasse over a shared exterior rolling shutter. It’s an old building, and the shutter mechanism covers both our storefronts. We couldn’t agree on a schedule for opening and closing it—I needed it up later for clients picking up repairs, she wanted it down earlier for security. We’d stopped speaking, and it was starting to affect our businesses and the mood of the whole block.

Glinda didn’t come in with a solution. She sat with each of us separately in our own shops, just asking questions about how our days worked and what we were worried about. Then she brought us together in her calm way and helped us hear what the other was actually saying. It wasn’t about the shutter; it was about predictability and respecting each other’s time. We worked out a seasonal schedule that changes with the daylight, and we wrote it down. A year later, that schedule still holds. More importantly, my neighbor and I can talk again.

What Glinda did for a pair of stubborn shopkeepers in Junction Quarter, she does every day for families, co-ops, and circles across the South Meadow and beyond. She fixes the human machinery so the rest of us can get on with our work. She’s a foundational part of what makes this network strong, and I hope you’ll agree she deserves this recognition.

Sincerely,
Amir Brook
Brook Device Repair

Nora Northcott: A Calmer Check-In

experience_leads.summary: Amir Brook, with Glinda Southwell's mediation, resolved a scheduling conflict with a neighboring bakery owner over a shared rolling shutter.

evidence.quote: We worked out a seasonal schedule that changes with the daylight, and we wrote it down. A year later, that schedule still holds.
evidence.context:
To the Founders’ Gala Selection Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Glinda Southwell for an honor at this year’s Gala. I know the network celebrates people who build connections and solve problems in practical ways, and I can’t think of anyone who embodies that more quietly and effectively than Glinda.

I speak from direct, somewhat awkward experience. Last spring, the owner of the bakery next to my repair shop and I were at a complete impasse over a shared exterior rolling shutter. It’s an old building, and the shutter mechanism covers both our storefronts. We couldn’t agree on a schedule for opening and closing it—I needed it up later for clients picking up repairs, she wanted it down earlier for security. We’d stopped speaking, and it was starting to affect our businesses and the mood of the whole block.

Glinda didn’t come in with a solution. She sat with each of us separately in our own shops, just asking questions about how our days worked and what we were worried about. Then she brought us together in her calm way and helped us hear what the other was actually saying. It wasn’t about the shutter; it was about predictability and respecting each other’s time. We worked out a seasonal schedule that changes with the daylight, and we wrote it down. A year later, that schedule still holds. More importantly, my neighbor and I can talk again.

What Glinda did for a pair of stubborn shopkeepers in Junction Quarter, she does every day for families, co-ops, and circles across the South Meadow and beyond. She fixes the human machinery so the rest of us can get on with our work. She’s a foundational part of what makes this network strong, and I hope you’ll agree she deserves this recognition.

Sincerely,
Amir Brook
Brook Device Repair

experience_leads.summary: Lydia Hart rewrote the entire orchard picking contract in plain language this past spring.

evidence.quote: prompted me to rewrite the entire orchard picking contract in plain language this past spring.
evidence.context:
To the Founders' Gala Selection Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Samuel Strawbridge for recognition at this year’s Gala. I manage the Eastfield Orchard Partnership, and Samuel runs our town’s adult literacy program. I’ve seen his work up close, and it’s made a real, practical difference here.

Last season, one of our regular seasonal pickers, a woman who’d been with us for years, started attending Samuel’s classes. She’d always relied on her daughter or a neighbor to read her the picking contract. Samuel used our contract—the old, dense one full of ‘heretofores’ and ‘parties of the first part’—as a lesson in his class. He didn’t just have them sound out the words; he asked them, ‘What do you need to understand from this? What’s fair?’ They picked it apart together.

A few weeks later, that picker came to my office. She brought her contract, pointed to the sections about pay scales and break times, and asked me two clear questions about them. She was reading it herself. She told me Samuel’s class taught her to ask those questions, that it wasn’t about being smart, it was about knowing what to look for. That moment changed how I saw my own work.

In fact, seeing Samuel’s class struggle with our legalese prompted me to rewrite the entire orchard picking contract in plain language this past spring. Samuel reviewed a draft for me. He said, ‘If your crew can’t read it, it’s not a good contract.’ Now the new version is clearer for everyone.

Samuel’s curious and patient. He never makes a big deal about what he does; he just asks people what they need to read and helps them find the confidence to do it. That quiet, persistent work builds a stronger foundation for all of us in Eastfield. He’s a founder in the truest sense—he helps people build their own capacity.

Thank you for your consideration,

Lydia Hart
Orchard Manager, Eastfield Orchard Partnership

He correctly identified it as a common, harmless fungus that appears in damp springs, preventing the beekeeper from applying an unnecessary and potentially harmful hive treatment.
   3.4. Bea Reedcombe (Community Health Worker) outlined a plan for the coming month. She intends to set up a small information stall at the next Hammerhead Rise market. The stall will distribute the latest Quadling Health Access newsletter and she will be available to answer questions about the upcoming seasonal flu shot program, including locations and times.

   - Dilys noted that Marcus's visual guide approach was an excellent example of simplifying access. She asked if Marcus would be willing to share the guide template, even if just as a photo, so other advice desks could adapt the idea.
   - Marcus agreed, noting he would need to create a new version without the copyrighted catalog images, perhaps using simple hand-drawn symbols.
   - Elspeth suggested that the genealogy request ledger system, while simple, could be adapted for other small-office tracking needs where a digital system is overkill.

   A3. Rowan Bell to circulate the one-page grant report template and a description of the genealogy ledger system to the broader ECLN network via the next digest.

6. Next Meeting
   The next quarterly meeting is scheduled for July 2024. Proposed agenda item: reviewing the impact of the simplified grant reporting template.

Meeting closed at 4:15 p.m.

experience_leads.summary: Spent an afternoon conducting a meticulous survey and photographic documentation of an eroded footpath boundary in the South Copse area.

evidence.quote: "I spent an afternoon there with a measuring line and a camera," Stone says.
evidence.context:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Emerald City Leadership Network
Wizard's Office Liaisons Circle
October 2025

This report outlines the activities supported by the October 2025 grant for the Wizard's Office Liaisons circle of the Emerald City Leadership Network. The funds were used to facilitate direct member engagement with civic infrastructure concerns, translating local observation into actionable administrative records.

In Bell Market ward, Councillor Abel Larkwood applied his portion of the grant to address a persistent community complaint. "The bench outside the post office had become unsafe," Larkwood reports. "The slats were cracked, and it was no longer a place where one could sit comfortably." After receiving a letter campaign organized by an elderly resident, Larkwood expedited the procurement process for a replacement. The new bench, constructed of durable treated timber, was installed within the month. He notes, "The administrative follow-through was streamlined by having a dedicated line item for such responsive, small-scale improvements."

Willa Rushwick, a council aide, focused on pedestrian safety near a school in her Spectacle Lane neighborhood. "Parents had been logging concerns with the precinct office for weeks," says Rushwick. "The intersection at the top of the lane sees a surge of carriages and bicycles right as children are arriving." Using the grant to cover the temporary assignment costs, Rushwick arranged for a crossing guard to be posted for one week during the morning rush. The presence not only ensured safety but also collected data on traffic patterns, which has been submitted to the city's traffic planning committee. "It was a short-term intervention," Rushwick explains, "but it created the evidentiary basis for discussing a more permanent solution."

In Quadling Country, survey assistant Nadia Stone utilized her allocation for fieldwork documentation. A footpath boundary in the South Copse area had been gradually eroded by seasonal runoff, washing away the original marker stones and creating confusion over the right-of-way. "I spent an afternoon there with a measuring line and a camera," Stone says. Her work was deliberately meticulous. "I distrust round numbers in survey work," she adds. "The record shows the precise degree of encroachment, the angle of the wash, and the locations of the remaining stone fragments." This clear, photographically supported record has been added to the parish maintenance file, providing the specific data required for any future repair or boundary restoration work.

The grant enabled these three Liaisons to act with a degree of administrative agility not always available through standard channels. Each project converted community input into a formal, documented civic request, demonstrating the value of bridging local observation with municipal process. The work remains unfinished in the sense that the data and precedents established are now part of ongoing civic discussions regarding maintenance, safety, and public space.

Timber Verge Repair Co-op
Founding Meeting Minutes
8 April 2024
Present: Martin Woodward, Arthur Keene, Ember Thistlewood, Gideon Pepperham. Rowan Bell, Community Manager, attended.

1. Purpose & Formation
Martin Woodward proposed forming a co-op to repair items that orchard villages cannot afford to replace, arguing that skilled repair extends the life of tools, furniture, and machines. The group agreed on the name Timber Verge Repair Co-op. Woodward was elected convener for a six-month term.

2. Fee Structure
After discussion, the co-op adopted a sliding-scale fee model. Fees will be based on the client's ability to pay and the complexity of the repair, with a minimum charge to cover basic materials. A fee schedule will be drafted before the next meeting.

3. Tools & Equipment
Arthur Keene offered the use of his personal joinery tools for a community furniture-repair bench. The offer was accepted unanimously. Keene noted the tools are suited for mortise-and-tenon joints and drawer-slide repairs.

Gideon Pepperham presented two sewing machines—a treadle model and a later electric—which he had already serviced and adjusted. These will form the core of a mending table. Pepperham confirmed both machines are in working order with fresh needles and bobbins.

4. Proposed Work Benches
Ember Thistlewood proposed establishing a dedicated bicycle-repair bench, to be set up in the summer months. She outlined a plan for basic tune-ups, flat-tire fixes, and brake adjustments. The bench would operate two afternoons per week, pending identification of a suitable covered outdoor space. This proposal was noted as a planned summer initiative.

5. Next Steps & Testing
Woodward emphasized that no setup is finished until it is tested. He will coordinate the transport of Keene's tools to the shared workshop space in the old Timber Verge lumber office. Pepperham will prepare a sign-up sheet for mending-table hours. Thistlewood will scout potential locations for the bicycle bench and report back in May.

The next meeting is scheduled for 6 May 2024.
Minutes recorded by Rowan Bell, Community Manager.

Rowan Bell · Community Manager · Timber Verge Repair Co-op debrief · June 2025

Post-meetup notes. Held at the South Meadow community hall. About fifteen attendees, a mix of co-op members and folks from the network's other circles who have an interest in woodwork, tools, or logistics.

Arthur Keene was there, of course, holding court by the tea urn. He didn't mention the dining table himself, but Hattie Tinstead brought it up. She said she’d heard from a neighbor in Quadling Country that Arthur had taken on a big old dining table missing its extension supports. The owner thought it was junk. Arthur apparently spent three days picking through scrap oak at the back of the Timber Verge yard, found pieces with the right grain, and hand-cut new supports so the leaf fits snug and doesn’t wobble. The neighbor is thrilled; says the table seats the whole family again. Arthur just nodded slowly and said, 'It’s all in the joint. A sliding dovetail, if you take your time, will outlast the tree it came from.' Then he launched into a story about a Gillikin cedar chest from sixty years ago.

Hattie Tinstead showed up with a canvas roll. She laid out a half-dozen pairs of fabric shears on the table. They were the ones from the Tinsmith Row community centre’s sewing group. She said last month the group was ready to throw them out, they were so dull they’d just chew fabric. She took them all, used a honing guide to get the angle right every time, and worked them on an oilstone. She demonstrated on one pair, cutting through a scrap of thick wool felt like it was butter. The shears are back in circulation. She mentioned she’s going to run a sharpening workshop at the tool library next quarter if there’s interest.

Talk of the tool library brought up Teo Brickholt’s name. A couple of people from the Brickway Transit Union said they’d heard Teo’s been instrumental in getting a neighborhood tool library started over in Green Market. He’s not just donating surplus hand tools—screwdrivers, wrenches, a couple of hand planes—from his hardware store, but he’s also been advising on the check-out system. He suggested a simple ledger and tags, something physical that doesn’t rely on everyone having a scroll-screen. They’re still in the planning stages, but they have a shelf unit and a donated lockbox now.

Dacey Barleybourne was in from Gillikin Falls. Gruff as ever, but had a good story. Said a delivery of rye came into the mill with higher moisture than usual. Could have sat and sweated, gone moldy in the silo. Instead of just processing it on the usual schedule, Dacey diverted the batch. Had the crew spread it all in the shallow storage bins overnight, cranked up the air circulation. Let it sit for a full day. They processed it the next morning, and the yield was fine. No must, no waste. Dacey said it was just paying attention. 'Grain tells you what it needs, if you listen.'

Abel Wickridge was the last to share. He drives freight out of Eastfield. Said there was a major snarl on the main Eastfield approach last Tuesday—a wagon lost a wheel, blocked both lanes. Dispatch was telling everyone to wait. Abel knew the schedule was tight for a load of milled timber headed to a framing crew in Emerald City. He remembered an old quarry road that cuts behind the hill. It’s rough, seldom-used, but passable if you take it slow. He took the detour, bumped along for forty minutes, and rejoined the Brickway past the blockage. Delivered the pallets only twenty minutes late. The foreman at the site didn’t even know there’d been a problem. Abel shrugged. 'Better a dusty truck than a missed deadline.'

Open actions from the meetup: Hattie will draft a date for the sharpening workshop and send it to the network calendar. A few folks asked if the tool library system Teo’s helping with could be a template for other neighborhoods; I’ll reach out to Teo to see if he’s willing to share notes. Arthur mentioned the co-op’s scrap pile is getting a bit too 'curated'—needs a proper sort-through. Dacey and Abel got talking about grain shipments and road conditions; might be a useful connection for the network’s logistics circle to follow up on.

Overall mood was focused and practical. Less about big ideas, more about the specific, tangible fixes people are doing in their own patches. Good energy.

evidence.quote: She received a donation of mixed walking aids from an estate clearance. Over three days last week, she sorted through the collection, inspecting each item.
evidence.context:
Quadling Health Access Coordinating Committee Minutes
Date: August 2025
Present: Rowan Bell (Community Manager, Emerald City Leadership Network), Wilhelmina Thistlewaite (Clinic manager, Bluebell Crossing Clinic), Odile Wickley (Health access navigator, Quadling Health Access), Orla Amberholt (Road crew foreman, Brickway Works), Mara Wells (Care equipment loan coordinator, North Orchard loan desk).

1. Call to Order
The meeting was called to order at 3:00 PM by Rowan Bell.

2. Updates from Members
2.1 Wilhelmina Thistlewaite (Billie) reported on her efforts regarding the Bluebell Crossing Clinic's communication systems. She is currently circulating a petition among local businesses in Bluebell Crossing and the surrounding Munchkin County townships. The petition aims to demonstrate community support for a grant application to fund a digital referral system. The goal is to replace the clinic's aging and unreliable fax machine, which frequently drops transmissions of patient referrals. Billie stated she has secured signatures from three local grocers and the owner of the Bluebell Inn so far.

2.2 Odile Wickley provided an update on her resource list project. She has completed a simple, updated list of pediatric dentists in the Emerald City and western Gillikin who offer income-based sliding scale fees. The list includes the practices' current contact information, eligibility requirements, and typical appointment lead times. She printed fifty copies for distribution at the North Orchard community center and the Quadling Health Access office in Redfern Hill. Initial feedback from two families last week confirmed that the information helped them schedule consultations.

2.3 Orla Amberholt reported on Brickway Works crew logistics. She is in the process of arranging a service agreement with a local industrial laundry in Redfern Hill. The plan is for the laundry to clean the road crew's soiled, high-visibility reflective vests on a monthly schedule. Orla stated this is intended to improve the vests' visibility for crew safety and to address crew concerns about wearing dirty gear, which she believes impacts morale. She is gathering quotes and will present a proposal to the Brickway Works administrative lead next week.

2.4 Mara Wells reported on inventory work at the North Orchard loan desk. She received a donation of mixed walking aids from an estate clearance. Over three days last week, she sorted through the collection, inspecting each item. She identified and tagged twelve adjustable aluminum canes and four four-wheeled rollators that met the loan desk's safety standards. These items have been moved to the cleaning station and are awaiting sterilization before being added to the active loan inventory.

3. Discussion and Coordination
3.1 Rowan Bell suggested Odile share a copy of the pediatric dentist list with Billie for the Bluebell Crossing Clinic's waiting room. Odile agreed to mail five copies.
3.2 Mara Wells asked if the industrial laundry service Orla is pursuing might be suitable for cleaning loaned medical equipment linens. Orla said she would inquire about capacity and rates for non-vest items and report back.
3.3 The group discussed the challenge of transporting equipment from the Quadling country to Gillikin for repairs. No immediate solution was identified, but Rowan agreed to raise it at the next Network transit circle meeting.

4. Action Items
- Wilhelmina Thistlewaite: Continue gathering petition signatures; aim for twenty by end of September.
- Odile Wickley: Mail five copies of the pediatric dentist list to Bluebell Crossing Clinic.
- Orla Amberholt: Finalize laundry service quotes and present proposal to Brickway Works admin.
- Mara Wells: Oversee the cleaning and intake process for the twelve canes and four rollators.
- Rowan Bell: Inquire about cross-country transport for medical equipment at the transit circle.

5. Next Meeting
The next meeting is scheduled for October 2025.

Meeting adjourned at 4:10 PM.

Nimmie

Post-event debrief: Meadow Mutual Aid Network Check-In, November 2025.

Attended: Ezra Hedgebourne (Blue Orchard), Sable Orchardfield (Eastfield), Odile Pepperby (Lantern Row), Calla Copperby (Bluebell Crossing), Briony Oakmere (Gate Quarter). Rowan Bell present as facilitator.

General atmosphere was energetic and positive. A lot of cross-pollination of ideas between different regions and types of work (care, transport, food, goods). Focus was on sharing what's been done lately and what's being looked at, no formal decisions required.

Item 1: Updates from the field.
- Ezra reported on the new mending sessions at the Blue Orchard community center. He connected a retired seamstress who wanted to help with the network. They've set up a weekly two-hour slot. In the first month, they repaired about twenty items—clothes, torn curtains, a backpack. It's become a social spot; a few people stay just to chat even if they don't have mending. Ezra emphasized the 'we' of it: 'We're keeping skills in the community and saving people a trip to the tailor.'
- Odile gave a quiet, dry update from Lantern Row. She worked directly with the pharmacy on Brickway that serves the care home. They used to deliver prescriptions on three different days depending on the supplier, which was confusing for staff and sometimes led to delays. Odile got them to consolidate to one dedicated delivery day. 'Now the boxes arrive, I sign for them, and the residents get their medications on time. It's not glamorous, but it prevents a dozen small crises a month.'
- Calla was very direct about the produce run. She set up an arrangement with the Quadling farmers market to collect unsold but still fresh produce at closing time. The first run was last week. Meadow Mutual Aid volunteers with carts met the vendors, loaded up, and distributed the food to forty families in Bluebell Crossing and the southern Emerald City precincts that same evening. 'No storage, no fuss. Food moved from where it was surplus to where it was needed in about three hours.'
- Briony described the coat drive initiative. She got permission to place a clearly marked bin at the front of her tram on the Gate Quarter-to-Market Square route. For one week, she made announcements and kept an eye on it. She collected over thirty gently used coats. 'People would get on, see the bin, and sometimes get off at the next stop to go home and fetch a coat. It was very simple.' The coats have been passed to the Mutual Aid network for sorting and distribution.

Item 2: Ideas in progress.
- Sable mentioned that other members of Meadow Mutual Aid have been talking to her about an idea. She's heard from several parents in the network that there's interest in a toy and book lending library. The Eastfield Childcare Co-op has a storage shed that isn't fully used. Sable is looking into the feasibility—what it would take to clean it out, set up shelves, and create a simple check-out system. She was clear: 'We're just at the looking-into-it stage. I'm hearing the need, so we're seeing if the co-op space can be part of the solution.'

Item 3: Open discussion and cross-connections.
- Ezra asked Briony if the tram collection could be a recurring thing, maybe for blankets in the deep winter. Briony said she'd ask her supervisor but thinks a weekend drive might be easier to manage than a full week.
- Odile asked Calla if the produce distribution included areas near care homes, suggesting some residents on fixed incomes might benefit. Calla said the current route doesn't but they can adjust; she'll get the route list to Odile to see if any stops align.
- Sable's library idea got a lot of positive murmurs. Ezra offered to connect her with the retired seamstress, who he said has a lot of children's books she's been meaning to find a home for.

Item 4: Next steps and actions.
- Calla will share the produce distribution route with Odile by end of week. (Action: Calla)
- Briony will inquire about a weekend blanket drive on the trams and report back. (Action: Briony)
- Sable will draft a simple proposal for the shed library to share with the co-op board and the wider network for feedback. (Action: Sable)
- Rowan to circulate these notes and check in on actions in December.

No major logistical hurdles identified. The group agreed to check in again in the new year, possibly with a focus on winter preparedness projects.

evidence.context:
To the Founders’ Gala Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Pia Oakridge of the Timber Verge Repair Co-op for recognition at this year’s Gala.

My own bit of context: I’m an electrician from Yellow Kiln. Last month, the collective there got a new pottery kiln, and the three-phase hookup was a mess. I rewired it to current code, got the inspectors in, and it passed without a hitch. It’s running now. That’s the sort of straightforward, necessary work our co-op does—fixing what’s broken so other work can happen.

But what Pia does is different. She’s the steward of our tool library. Last fall, someone donated a vintage hand planer. It was rusty, the blade was dull, and the adjustment knob was seized. Most folks would’ve tossed it in the scrap pile. Pia took it home. She spent evenings cleaning every part, sharpening the iron, and oiling the mechanisms. She didn’t just make it work; she made it a pleasure to use.

That tool is now one of the most requested items in the library. People are using it for furniture projects, for trim work, for all sorts of fine woodworking. They come back raving about how smooth it cuts. Pia’s work turns a piece of forgotten history into a community asset. It’s not flashy, but it’s essential. She understands that a well-maintained tool doesn’t just perform a task—it teaches respect for the craft.

In a network that talks a lot about building and repairing, Pia Oakridge embodies the quiet, foundational work that makes the rest possible. She has my full support for this nomination.

Sincerely,
Cyrus Poppymere
Poppymere Electrical
Timber Verge Repair Co-op

experience_leads.summary: Adapted to a road closure by proposing and testing a detour via a narrow service lane, keeping the bus route running only about two minutes behind schedule.

evidence.quote: I proposed it to the dispatcher, we did a test run to be sure, and we used it for the duration.
evidence.context: Goldenway's cobbles were due for repair, which meant my usual route for the 47 was completely blocked for three days. The official detour would have added twelve minutes each way, which doesn't sound like much until you multiply it by thirty-odd trips a day and a bus full of people trying to get to work or appointments. I remembered a narrow service lane that runs behind the old mill—it's tight, but it's paved and connects back to the main road. I proposed it to the dispatcher, we did a test run to be sure, and we used it for the duration. We had to go slow and give way to the occasional delivery cart, but we kept the route running only about two minutes behind schedule. The passengers appreciated the consistency. Sometimes the best solution isn't the official one, it's the one that keeps things moving.

experience_leads.summary: Zinnia Pepperdale recorded an oral history interview with a retired sign painter.

evidence.quote: where I had the privilege of recording an oral history with a retired sign painter from the Brickway district. We talked for nearly two hours
evidence.context:
To the Founders' Gala Nomination Committee,

I am writing to nominate Maren Crowmere for recognition at this year's Gala. I know we're all asked to think about impact, and sometimes that's a grand gesture. More often, it's the quiet work that keeps the wheels turning. My own recent work has been in the Lantern Row Reading Room, where I had the privilege of recording an oral history with a retired sign painter from the Brickway district. We talked for nearly two hours about mixing paints that last through the Emerald City's damp winters and how to hold a lettering brush for a clean serif. It felt important, capturing a craft that isn't really taught in the same way anymore. But that recording now sits in a drawer, waiting for someone to organize it, to make it accessible. That's where Maren's work comes in.

While I was occupied with that one conversation, Maren was in the Gate Quarter Reading Room, dealing with the flood of donations that always comes after the spring cleaning festivals. She took on three full boxes of magazines—gardening, mechanics, crafts—that had been left on the step. She didn't just stack them. She sorted them by year and topic, repaired torn spines with tape, and shelved them in the periodicals section. Now, when someone comes in looking for ideas to fix a bicycle chain or plan a window box, those resources are right there, easy to find.

This is Maren's gift. She sees the immediate need—the clutter on the floor, the patron looking frustrated—and she addresses it with a clear, patient focus. She makes the knowledge we work so hard to preserve actually usable. My recording is a potential resource; Maren's sorting made resources available that same afternoon. She builds the practical foundation that lets the rest of us do our more specialized work. For her consistent, essential contribution to making the Reading Rooms functional and welcoming places, I wholeheartedly nominate Maren Crowmere.

Sincerely,
Zinnia Pepperdale
Oral History Volunteer, Reading Room Network

evidence.context:
Wizard's Office Liaisons Circle
Meeting Minutes
Date: 12 June 2025
Present: Magnus Greendale, Heath Gatecombe, Tomas Saffronley, Coralie Greenshaw, Mott Peppercombe, Juniper Hazelby, Rowan Bell (Community Manager)

1. Welcome and Opening Remarks
Rowan Bell opened the meeting at 7:05 p.m. The agenda was accepted without amendment.

2. Review of Member Actions and Updates
2.1 Magnus Greendale reported on his work to revise the instructions for requesting a replacement household recycling bin. The new instructions are clearer and now include a simple diagram. He noted that the average call time to the civic works department for this issue has decreased by two minutes since the change. A clerk from the department confirmed the reduction.

2.2 Heath Gatecombe provided an update on his proposal for the Brickway Junction library branch. He plans to advocate for the installation of an after-hours book return drop box. The request will be framed to accommodate residents who work during the library's open hours. He will prepare a formal proposal for the next Library Advisory Board meeting.

2.3 Tomas Saffronley reported on the completion of a small civic grant project in Cobble Ford. The grant, which he facilitated, allowed the hamlet to repair a historic stone well cover that had become a safety hazard. The work is finished, and the well is now safely covered.

2.4 Coralie Greenshaw shared that she has created a simple glossary explaining common healthcare terms like 'co-pay' and 'referral' in plain language. It is a single laminated sheet. Three Quadling clinics are now keeping copies at their front desks. She noted that several patients have commented that it helps them understand their paperwork better.

2.5 Mott Peppercombe gave a brief report from the Brickway Works bridge crew. He stated that his crew recently used a quick-set concrete mix to fill and level a cracked concrete approach slab on a little-used farm track bridge near Bluebell Crossing. The work was done to prevent further deterioration from water ingress. The repair is holding.

2.6 Regarding Juniper Hazelby, Magnus Greendale mentioned that he and others had heard about her contribution to last year's Gillikin Light Festival. He said the word among liaisons was that Juniper provided the precise metal framework for a large kinetic sculpture that was a centerpiece of the event. Juniper Hazelby confirmed she had worked on the project but noted the framework was a subcontract from the main fabricator. She did not elaborate further.

3. Discussion: Improving Communication Between Offices and Residents
3.1 Magnus Greendale initiated a discussion on the persistent issue of public notices being written in overly formal language. He stated, "We get fewer complaints when the words are simpler. My recycling bin project proved that. But getting other departments to adopt the practice is slow."

3.2 Coralie Greenshaw agreed, relating it to her glossary work. "People shouldn't need a translator for basic services," she said.

3.3 Heath Gatecombe suggested that liaisons could compile examples of successful plain-language revisions from their respective areas to create a shared resource. Tomas Saffronley noted that such a resource would need approval from the central communications office to be used widely.

3.4 Juniper Hazelby asked Tomas to repeat the point about central office approval. After he did, she said, "Right. So we'd need a spec for that resource before we build it."

3.5 Action: Magnus Greendale and Coralie Greenshaw will draft two or three examples of revised public notices/forms for review at the next meeting.

4. Liaison Support Requests
4.1 Mott Peppercombe raised an issue about the standard forms for reporting minor bridge wear. He finds the current form has too many fields irrelevant to initial field assessment. "My crew spots a crack, they need to log the location and size, not write an essay on drainage patterns from five years ago. That comes later."

4.2 Tomas Saffronley said he would inquire about the possibility of a simplified 'field observation' version of the form. Heath Gatecombe offered to provide feedback from the ward perspective on what information is most critical for initial reporting.

4.3 Action: Tomas Saffronley will follow up with the Infrastructure Forms office and report back.

5. Any Other Business
5.1 Rowan Bell reminded the group of the Network's Summer Social on July 20th.

5.2 Juniper Hazelby asked if there was a standard process for liaisons to share technical specifications for public works projects across regions (e.g., bridge components, signage brackets). A brief discussion confirmed there is not a formal channel. Tomas Saffronley suggested this could be added to the agenda for a future meeting focused on inter-regional projects.

6. Next Meeting
Agreed for Wednesday, 10 July 2025, at 7:00 p.m. at the Emerald City Chamber meeting room.

Meeting adjourned at 8:30 p.m.
Minutes recorded by Rowan Bell.

evidence.context:
Winkie Works Guild
Monthly Business Meeting
May 2025

Present: Tilda Poppyley, Reuben Brookcombe, Lena Kilnfield, Rowan Bell (Community Manager, non-voting).

1. Call to Order
Meeting called to order at 7:05 PM. No reading of previous minutes as copies were circulated via the Yellow Brick Board.

2. Recent Member Projects
Members shared updates on recent hands-on work.

   a) Tilda Poppyley reported on a fabrication project completed last month. A Winkie community greenhouse required a wide rainwater collection gutter. She formed a continuous channel from a single roll of salvaged galvanized steel, eliminating seams and potential leak points. The gutter is now installed and functioning.

   b) Reuben Brookcombe described a repair for a small grain mill in the western Winkie Country. The mill's sorting conveyor belt had a broken pulley wheel. Reuben machined a custom-sized replacement from stock on hand. From receiving the call to having the mill operational again took two days.

   c) Lena Kilnfield shared a small repair completed at the Gate Quarter school library. The book return cart had a cracked caster, making it difficult to move. She identified a compatible spare part from a broken office chair slated for disposal. The cart is now back in service, and the school avoided a maintenance call-out fee.

3. Discussion: Skills-Sharing Session Proposal
Rowan Bell proposed the Guild consider hosting a practical skills-sharing session for the wider network later in the year. The idea would be to demonstrate basic metalworking, simple machining, and repair techniques applicable to small businesses and community spaces.

   - Reuben Brookcombe stated he would be willing to demonstrate basic lathe safety and how to turn a simple bushing, provided the session was kept small for safety.
   - Tilda Poppyley agreed in principle but emphasized the need for a very clear scope and proper liability waivers if anyone other than members were to handle tools.
   - Lena Kilnfield suggested pairing demonstrations with a 'repair clinic' format, where people could bring a single, small broken item for assessment, not necessarily for on-the-spot repair. This could help manage expectations and volume.

4. Action Items
   - ACTION (Rowan Bell): To draft a one-page proposal for a skills-sharing session, incorporating the repair clinic idea and liability considerations, for review at the June meeting.
   - ACTION (All Members): To think of 2-3 specific, safe, and beginner-appropriate tasks that could be demonstrated in a 20-minute slot.

5. Other Business
   - Reuben raised the issue of consistent supply for certain tool steel grades. Tilda noted a supplier in Timber Verge that she uses. They agreed to exchange contact details after the meeting.
   - Lena asked if the Guild had a small budget for a shared reference library, such as manuals or material spec sheets. Rowan will investigate if network micro-grant funds could be applied for this purpose and report back.

6. Next Meeting
Scheduled for June 10, 2025, at 7:00 PM at the Westgate Foundry meeting room.

Meeting adjourned at 8:20 PM.

The next guild meeting is scheduled for June 11, 2024, at the South Copse Dental Practice community room.

FOR RELEASE

EMERALD CITY, Oz – April 2024 – The Emerald City Leadership Network today highlighted the practical, community-focused work of members from its Young Founders Circle. From accessible transit to sustainable shopping and hands-on skill-building, these founders demonstrate that impactful leadership often lies in thoughtful, everyday actions.

Leif Emeryholt, a ticket office supervisor with Emerald City Tramways in Violet Hills, recently introduced a daily quiet hour at his station. From 2 to 3 p.m., the overhead lights are dimmed and intercom announcements are paused. 'We noticed many travelers, especially those navigating complex routes or managing anxiety, found the constant noise and glare overwhelming,' Emeryholt explained. 'This small adjustment creates a calmer point of service. Several regulars now plan their trips around that hour, and we’ve seen a noticeable decrease in tension at the counter during that time.'

In the heart of the Emerald City, Reuben Spindlecombe of the Spectacle Lane Refill Shop focuses on removing friction for customers seeking low-waste goods. Last month, a large shipment of jute garden twine arrived in a hopelessly tangled knot. 'It was a proper bird’s nest,' Spindlecombe said, his words tumbling out. 'Could have sent it back, but that’s waste. So I spent a slow Tuesday afternoon just… untangling. Rewound it all onto our meter spools. Now customers can buy exactly what they need, cleanly, and nothing’s wasted. It’s not glamorous, but it’s the job.'

Across the Munchkin Country in Brickway Junction, Dinah Haywick co-founded the Brickway Junction Makers Space to put tools and skills into community hands. Last weekend, she led a workshop on crafting simple three-legged stools. 'We used offcuts of ash from a local flooring company—beautiful wood that would’ve been scrap,' Haywick said briskly. 'Twelve people went home with a sturdy stool and the confidence to make another. It’s about demystifying the process. If you can measure, drill, and glue, you can build something that lasts.'

Rowan Bell, Community Manager for the Network, noted the common thread. 'These aren’t headline-grabbing ventures, but they are deeply considered. Leif creates accessibility through quiet, Reuben through perseverance, and Dinah through shared knowledge. They’re each building a slightly more usable, less wasteful, and more skilled Oz, one quiet hour, one spool of twine, one stool at a time.'

The Emerald City Leadership Network connects members across Oz through circles focused on transit, mutual aid, business, craft, and community health. The Young Founders Circle supports emerging enterprise leaders under 40.

experience_leads.summary: Enid compiled and posted a printed, large-print roster with time slots for the annual flu shot clinic in Hammerhead Rise, which was used successfully, calming the atmosphere and reducing wait times.

evidence.quote: I compiled a printed, large-print roster with fifteen-minute time slots for the whole access day. We posted copies at the community board and the library a week ahead.
evidence.context:
From: Enid Hazelstead (Quadling Health Access)
To: Festival Committee
Subject: Re: Autumn Outreach - Item Updates
Date: September 18, 2024

Hello everyone,

Milo, that’s a lovely offer for Violet Hills.

On our end, the annual flu shot clinic in Hammerhead Rise is done. We tried something new this year. I compiled a printed, large-print roster with fifteen-minute time slots for the whole access day. We posted copies at the community board and the library a week ahead. People could come by my desk, look at the sheet, and put their name in a slot that worked for them.

It made a real difference. On the day, there was no usual morning queue snaking out the door. People arrived closer to their time, the nurses had a steady flow, and the whole atmosphere was much calmer. An older passenger told me it was the first time she didn’t have to stand for an hour waiting. We’ll definitely do the roster again.

Warmly,
Enid

evidence.quote: So I started a rule that every donation gets a clear date label right when it’s dropped off. It’s simple, but folks follow it now, and waste is way down.
evidence.context:
To the Founders’ Gala Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Barnaby Stonefield from Meadow Mutual Aid for a recognition award. I see his work from my end, as the keeper of the Bluebell Crossing community fridge. This nomination comes out of my own small lesson in order: a few months back, I had to clear out a whole shelf of food that had gone past its good date. It was heartbreaking. So I started a rule that every donation gets a clear date label right when it’s dropped off. It’s simple, but folks follow it now, and waste is way down.

That little system works because people like Barnaby get the food to us reliably. He’s the delivery rota lead, and his job is all about quiet, practical solutions when things go wrong. Back in the fall, our Thursday circuit was thrown into chaos. The usual shortcut through Reed Flats was shut for roadworks without any warning. For most of us, that just means a detour. For Barnaby, it meant an entire insulated delivery route was about to fail—if those boxes sat in the cart too long, the cooler packs would thaw and everything inside would spoil.

He didn’t just send a message saying there’d be delays. He replanned the whole Thursday circuit on the spot, figuring out a new sequence that added forty minutes of travel but kept every stop on time. He coordinated with the drivers, recalculated the ice-pack timelines, and made sure not a single delivery was missed or warmed. I know because our box arrived, cold as ever, right when it always does.

That’s Barnaby. No drama, just a slightly weary voice on the com-line working the problem until it’s solved. He makes sure the aid gets through, so the rest of us can do our part. He embodies what Meadow Mutual Aid is all about. Please consider him for this honor.

Sincerely,
Lena Thistlecombe
Bluebell Crossing Community Fridge

experience_leads.summary: Oriel Brambleworth designed and built a folding puppet booth for the Quadling Health Access group, which was used in December to demonstrate hand-washing routines to children.

evidence.quote: At their request, he designed and built a folding puppet booth for use at community health fairs. The booth was used in December to demonstrate hand-washing routines to children.
evidence.context:
Festival Committee Meeting
Date: January 16, 2025
Present: Ulric Stoneshaw, Oriel Brambleworth, Dacey Brambleley, Rowan Bell (Community Manager)

1. Call to Order
   The meeting was called to order at 7:00 PM at the Workshop on Lantern Row.

2. Storage and Logistics
   Ulric Stoneshaw raised the issue of time lost at the start of each festival season locating materials. He proposed a reorganization of the primary storage shed on Lantern Row. His plan involves acquiring a set of rolling bins, each to be clearly labeled for specific hardware (nails, screws, hinges) and fabric rolls. He stated this would allow crews to pull out only what they need and quickly return items, rather than digging through stacked crates. No action was taken; further discussion on sourcing bins is planned for the February meeting.

3. Member Project Updates
   3.1 Oriel Brambleworth reported on a completed project for the Quadling Health Access group. At their request, he designed and built a folding puppet booth for use at community health fairs. The booth was used in December to demonstrate hand-washing routines to children. Oriel noted the booth folds flat for transport in a cart and sets up in under five minutes. He used a lightweight frame from the Timber Verge Repair Co-op and canvas remnants from last year's Festival banners.

   3.2 Dacey Brambleley provided an update on a fabrication project for the Gillikin Growers circle. She was approached by a greenhouse operator struggling to manually adjust roof vents across a long structure. Dacey created a prototype bracket from aluminum stock. The bracket allows a standard small motor, attached to a simple pulley system, to automate the opening and closing of the vents. The prototype was installed at a greenhouse in northern Gillikin for a three-day test in late December and performed without failure. Dacey noted the design uses common machine shop parts to keep future replication simple and affordable.

4. Old Business
   There was no old business.

5. New Business
   Rowan Bell inquired if the puppet booth design or vent bracket prototype could be documented for the network's shared project library. Both Oriel and Dacey agreed to provide basic sketches and a parts list by the end of February.

6. Next Meeting
   The next meeting is scheduled for February 20, 2025, at the Workshop on Lantern Row.

7. Adjournment
   The meeting was adjourned at 8:15 PM.

Minutes submitted by Rowan Bell, Community Manager.

evidence.quote: Leif Emeryholt, a ticket office supervisor with Emerald City Tramways in Violet Hills, recently introduced a daily quiet hour at his station. From 2 to 3 p.m., the overhead lights are dimmed and intercom announcements are paused.
evidence.context:
FOR RELEASE

EMERALD CITY, Oz – April 2024 – The Emerald City Leadership Network today highlighted the practical, community-focused work of members from its Young Founders Circle. From accessible transit to sustainable shopping and hands-on skill-building, these founders demonstrate that impactful leadership often lies in thoughtful, everyday actions.

Leif Emeryholt, a ticket office supervisor with Emerald City Tramways in Violet Hills, recently introduced a daily quiet hour at his station. From 2 to 3 p.m., the overhead lights are dimmed and intercom announcements are paused. 'We noticed many travelers, especially those navigating complex routes or managing anxiety, found the constant noise and glare overwhelming,' Emeryholt explained. 'This small adjustment creates a calmer point of service. Several regulars now plan their trips around that hour, and we’ve seen a noticeable decrease in tension at the counter during that time.'

In the heart of the Emerald City, Reuben Spindlecombe of the Spectacle Lane Refill Shop focuses on removing friction for customers seeking low-waste goods. Last month, a large shipment of jute garden twine arrived in a hopelessly tangled knot. 'It was a proper bird’s nest,' Spindlecombe said, his words tumbling out. 'Could have sent it back, but that’s waste. So I spent a slow Tuesday afternoon just… untangling. Rewound it all onto our meter spools. Now customers can buy exactly what they need, cleanly, and nothing’s wasted. It’s not glamorous, but it’s the job.'

Across the Munchkin Country in Brickway Junction, Dinah Haywick co-founded the Brickway Junction Makers Space to put tools and skills into community hands. Last weekend, she led a workshop on crafting simple three-legged stools. 'We used offcuts of ash from a local flooring company—beautiful wood that would’ve been scrap,' Haywick said briskly. 'Twelve people went home with a sturdy stool and the confidence to make another. It’s about demystifying the process. If you can measure, drill, and glue, you can build something that lasts.'

Rowan Bell, Community Manager for the Network, noted the common thread. 'These aren’t headline-grabbing ventures, but they are deeply considered. Leif creates accessibility through quiet, Reuben through perseverance, and Dinah through shared knowledge. They’re each building a slightly more usable, less wasteful, and more skilled Oz, one quiet hour, one spool of twine, one stool at a time.'

The Emerald City Leadership Network connects members across Oz through circles focused on transit, mutual aid, business, craft, and community health. The Young Founders Circle supports emerging enterprise leaders under 40.

   The meeting opened at 6:05 PM in the Wizard's Office Annex, Conference Room B. Rowan Bell welcomed everyone and noted the aim of the meeting was to share updates and coordinate on workflows between the Wizard's Office and community networks.

2. Community Records Archiving (South Copse)
   Elspeth Wickham reported on the completion of a long-term archiving project for the South Copse community council. She sorted three decades of community meeting minutes by topic into labeled binders. The topics included road maintenance, drainage disputes, and public space allocations. A council member from South Copse has already used the new system to quickly reference the 1998 decision on gravel versus hardtop for a secondary lane, which informed a current repair discussion.

3. Permitting Process Review
   Ivy Coppermore provided an update on a recent permit application for the Reading Room Network's mobile library van. She reviewed the request for the van to park in three Emerald City neighborhoods: Spectacle Lane, Lantern Row, and near the Fountain Plaza. Ivy verified the vehicle's dimensions against the specific street-width regulations for each proposed parking zone, confirming the van would not impede the Brickway transit lanes or emergency access in any of the locations. The permit was approved with standard operating conditions.

4. Grant Administration and Recipient Support
   Frey Hazeldale outlined plans for improving grant reporting. He is planning a half-day workshop for current and prospective grant recipients, focusing on how to define and measure tangible project outcomes. The workshop will move beyond simply listing expenditures to help groups articulate what change they aim to create and how they will know it has been achieved. A draft agenda and potential dates in late September or early October were circulated for feedback.
   Bea Reedcombe shared a related example from the field. She recently helped a family in Westgate Mills complete a Wizard's Office Home Accessibility Grant application for a wheelchair ramp. Bea walked them through the required specifications, including the necessary slope measurements, and assisted in collecting three quotes from local contractors as mandated by the grant guidelines. The application was submitted successfully.

5. Open Discussion and Coordination
   A discussion followed on how to better connect grant applicants with the record-keeping resources Elspeth has organized. It was suggested that a brief guide to locating past community decisions could be added to the grant application packet for rural projects.

6. Actions and Next Steps
   - Frey Hazeldale to finalize the workshop agenda and proposed dates by September 10th and share with the group for dissemination to their respective networks.
   - Elspeth Wickham and Bea Reedcombe to collaborate on a one-page guide on "Finding Past Community Decisions" for grant applicants, due for review at the next meeting.
   - Ivy Coppermore to note the successful library van permit as a model case for future multi-location mobile service applications.
   - Next meeting scheduled for October 2024.

Meeting adjourned at 7:20 PM.

Pella

experience_leads.summary: Reported that when a delivery of rye with higher moisture than usual came into the mill, diverted the batch, had the crew spread it in shallow storage bins overnight with increased air circulation, processed it the next morning, resulting in fine yield with no waste.

evidence.quote: Said a delivery of rye came into the mill with higher moisture than usual. Could have sat and sweated, gone moldy in the silo. evidence.context:
Rowan Bell · Community Manager · Timber Verge Repair Co-op debrief · June 2025

Post-meetup notes. Held at the South Meadow community hall. About fifteen attendees, a mix of co-op members and folks from the network's other circles who have an interest in woodwork, tools, or logistics.

Arthur Keene was there, of course, holding court by the tea urn. He didn't mention the dining table himself, but Hattie Tinstead brought it up. She said she’d heard from a neighbor in Quadling Country that Arthur had taken on a big old dining table missing its extension supports. The owner thought it was junk. Arthur apparently spent three days picking through scrap oak at the back of the Timber Verge yard, found pieces with the right grain, and hand-cut new supports so the leaf fits snug and doesn’t wobble. The neighbor is thrilled; says the table seats the whole family again. Arthur just nodded slowly and said, 'It’s all in the joint. A sliding dovetail, if you take your time, will outlast the tree it came from.' Then he launched into a story about a Gillikin cedar chest from sixty years ago.

Hattie Tinstead showed up with a canvas roll. She laid out a half-dozen pairs of fabric shears on the table. They were the ones from the Tinsmith Row community centre’s sewing group. She said last month the group was ready to throw them out, they were so dull they’d just chew fabric. She took them all, used a honing guide to get the angle right every time, and worked them on an oilstone. She demonstrated on one pair, cutting through a scrap of thick wool felt like it was butter. The shears are back in circulation. She mentioned she’s going to run a sharpening workshop at the tool library next quarter if there’s interest.

Talk of the tool library brought up Teo Brickholt’s name. A couple of people from the Brickway Transit Union said they’d heard Teo’s been instrumental in getting a neighborhood tool library started over in Green Market. He’s not just donating surplus hand tools—screwdrivers, wrenches, a couple of hand planes—from his hardware store, but he’s also been advising on the check-out system. He suggested a simple ledger and tags, something physical that doesn’t rely on everyone having a scroll-screen. They’re still in the planning stages, but they have a shelf unit and a donated lockbox now.

Dacey Barleybourne was in from Gillikin Falls. Gruff as ever, but had a good story. Said a delivery of rye came into the mill with higher moisture than usual. Could have sat and sweated, gone moldy in the silo. Instead of just processing it on the usual schedule, Dacey diverted the batch. Had the crew spread it all in the shallow storage bins overnight, cranked up the air circulation. Let it sit for a full day. They processed it the next morning, and the yield was fine. No must, no waste. Dacey said it was just paying attention. 'Grain tells you what it needs, if you listen.'

Abel Wickridge was the last to share. He drives freight out of Eastfield. Said there was a major snarl on the main Eastfield approach last Tuesday—a wagon lost a wheel, blocked both lanes. Dispatch was telling everyone to wait. Abel knew the schedule was tight for a load of milled timber headed to a framing crew in Emerald City. He remembered an old quarry road that cuts behind the hill. It’s rough, seldom-used, but passable if you take it slow. He took the detour, bumped along for forty minutes, and rejoined the Brickway past the blockage. Delivered the pallets only twenty minutes late. The foreman at the site didn’t even know there’d been a problem. Abel shrugged. 'Better a dusty truck than a missed deadline.'

Open actions from the meetup: Hattie will draft a date for the sharpening workshop and send it to the network calendar. A few folks asked if the tool library system Teo’s helping with could be a template for other neighborhoods; I’ll reach out to Teo to see if he’s willing to share notes. Arthur mentioned the co-op’s scrap pile is getting a bit too 'curated'—needs a proper sort-through. Dacey and Abel got talking about grain shipments and road conditions; might be a useful connection for the network’s logistics circle to follow up on.

Overall mood was focused and practical. Less about big ideas, more about the specific, tangible fixes people are doing in their own patches. Good energy.

To the Founders’ Gala Committee,

I’m writing to nominate Ines Emeryby for this year’s recognition. I’ve gotten to know her through the Quadling Health Access circle, and I’ve been consistently impressed by how she identifies a need and finds a practical, kind way to meet it.

She builds the trust needed to make these things happen, turning a health access idea into a tangible service for dozens of families. She embodies the spirit of quiet, effective community care that this network celebrates.

Sincerely,
Ines Spindleton

Festival Committee
Meeting Minutes
Date: November 26, 2024
Present: Rowan Bell (Community Manager, Secretary), Pim Plumstead, Julian Park, Quill Tincombe, Mabry Rushcombe

1. Welcome and Updates
   Rowan Bell welcomed members and called the meeting to order at 6:05 PM at the Chamber Hall annex. The minutes from the October meeting were approved.

2. Project Reports
   2.1. Accessibility in Performance Costumes
   Pim Plumstead reported on adapting a knight's tabard for a wheelchair-using actor in the upcoming Brickway Players production. The standard side seams were replaced with a series of magnetic closures, allowing the actor to remove and replace the costume unaided during a standard 15-minute intermission. A prototype was completed last week and approved by the actor and the stage manager. Pim noted the magnets are sewn into a reinforced channel and covered with a matching fabric flap for safety and aesthetics.

   2.2. Puppet Repair Clinic
   Quill Tincombe summarized the free puppet repair clinic held on November 12 at the Lantern Row community center. He repaired seventeen puppets over four hours, with common issues being torn seams on felt animals and loose wooden dowel joints on marionettes. Quill mentioned one parent brought in a puppet that had been chewed by a family pet, which required a full replacement of the head's internal stuffing and a careful patch job. He used materials from his own workshop and said the event was 'a lovely bit of chaos, with children watching wide-eyed as their friends came back to life.'

   3.1. Modular Storage System
   Julian Park presented initial sketches for modular storage racks designed for the Committee's shared warehouse space. The concept involves interlocking wooden frames that can be configured to hold folded tents, tables of varying lengths, and rolled banners. Julian is planning to source reclaimed timber from the Timber Verge Repair Co-op and hopes to have a working prototype by mid-December for committee feedback. This is a planned project awaiting final measurements of the warehouse bay.

   3.2. Community Banner Workshop
   Mabry Rushcombe proposed a public workshop to create a large patchwork banner commemorating the Emerald City's founding anniversary. The plan is to invite residents to bring fabric scraps and contribute a stitched square under guidance. Mabry envisions the banner being completed over a series of weekend sessions in Gate Quarter early next year and displayed during the anniversary festivities. This is a planned initiative; Mabry will draft a materials list and potential venue options for the next meeting.

4. Logistics and Scheduling
   The next Festival Committee meeting is scheduled for December 17, 2024. Rowan Bell will check the availability of the Chamber Hall annex.
   Action Items:
   - Julian Park: Finalize warehouse measurements and produce a cost estimate for the modular storage prototype by Dec 10.
   - Mabry Rushcombe: Develop a draft schedule and material requirements for the banner workshop for review at the next meeting.
   - Rowan Bell: Circulate contact information for the Brickway Transit Union regarding potential transport of banner materials.

5. Other Business
   Pim mentioned that Spectacle Lane has a surplus of green velvet off-cuts from a recent project and offered them for the banner workshop. Mabry accepted the offer.
   Quill inquired about liability insurance for public repair clinics; Rowan agreed to look into the network's coverage.
   Meeting adjourned at 7:20 PM.

Respectfully submitted,
Rowan Bell
Community Manager, Emerald City Leadership Network

experience_leads.summary: Set up a lockable cash box with a slot and a logbook for the repair cafe's donation tracking.

evidence.quote: She set up a simple lockable cash box with a slot and a logbook next to it. Now, when they open the box to bank the donations, they record the date and amount in the book.
evidence.context:
Small Business Circle debrief. Rowan Bell, Community Manager. November 2025. Present: Bram Meadowholt, Marlo Meadowmere, Minna Winkleworth, Mabel Brambleshaw, Cecily Cinderdale. Meeting held over voice call.

The main topic was the regular check-in on 'what you saw and fixed.' Each person shared one thing from the last few weeks. The aim was to highlight the kind of small, practical work that keeps a business or a community function running without fanfare.

Bram Meadowholt went first. He said he was reviewing payroll for a three-person carpentry crew he does the books for. He caught a duplicate entry before the funds were sent. If it had gone through, the recovery process would have taken weeks. He said, 'It was just a line I'd seen twice. The amounts matched exactly.' He corrected it and sent the single payment.

Marlo Meadowmere talked about his barbershop. He said Saturday afternoons can be slow. A musician from Reed Flats, a regular customer, mentioned needing a place to try out some new pieces. Marlo offered the shop. They moved two waiting chairs aside next to the big front window. He didn't advertise, just told a few neighbors and put a small sign on the door. About a dozen people came, some just walking in off the street. He said, 'It wasn't a concert, just a fellow with a guitar. But it felt nice. And I did three haircuts for people who wandered in to listen.'

Minna Winkleworth described her work at the foundry. She'd been watching the flow at three finishing benches. Workers were going back and forth too much for different grits of abrasive and specific tools. Over a shift break, she repositioned the storage racks and tool caddies. She estimated it saves a few minutes per item processed. She said, 'It's not a redesign. Just putting the coarse stuff closer to the coarse work, the fine stuff by the fine work. Less walking.'

Mabel Brambleshaw was on a long haul toward the Emerald City. At a rest stop, she did her walk-around and saw a puddle under her rig. It was coolant, a slow leak from a hose. She had a spare jug of coolant in the cab. She topped up the reservoir to get to her scheduled layover, then called ahead to the garage there to confirm they had the right hose in stock. She said, 'If you ignore a small leak, it becomes a big one. Then you're stuck on the Brickway waiting for a tow, and everyone's schedule is wrecked.'

Cecily Cinderdale was asked by the local repair cafe to look at their donation system. They had a tin that people put coins in for tool maintenance, but they never knew how much they had month-to-month. She set up a simple lockable cash box with a slot and a logbook next to it. Now, when they open the box to bank the donations, they record the date and amount in the book. She said, 'It's not a ledger, but it's a record. Now they can see if a busy month means more funds for buying a new set of drivers.'

No formal action items came from the circle. The tone was matter-of-fact. The value seemed to be in stating these things out loud to peers. Bram was hesitant, asking if his example was 'the right kind of thing.' Others affirmed it was exactly the point. Minna noted that her change was small, but 'small things add up across a shift.' Mabel agreed.

I will note for the network log that these are examples of operational vigilance and local adaptation. No funding or network-wide coordination was requested. The circle plans to continue these check-ins bi-monthly.

-Rowan Bell
