Meeting Minutes
Date: 12 June 2025
Present: Magnus Greendale, Heath Gatecombe, Tomas Saffronley, Coralie Greenshaw, Mott Peppercombe, Juniper Hazelby, Rowan Bell (Community Manager)

1. Welcome and Opening Remarks
Rowan Bell opened the meeting at 7:05 p.m. The agenda was accepted without amendment.

2. Review of Member Actions and Updates
2.1 Magnus Greendale reported on his work to revise the instructions for requesting a replacement household recycling bin. The new instructions are clearer and now include a simple diagram. He noted that the average call time to the civic works department for this issue has decreased by two minutes since the change. A clerk from the department confirmed the reduction.

2.2 Heath Gatecombe provided an update on his proposal for the Brickway Junction library branch. He plans to advocate for the installation of an after-hours book return drop box. The request will be framed to accommodate residents who work during the library's open hours. He will prepare a formal proposal for the next Library Advisory Board meeting.

2.3 Tomas Saffronley reported on the completion of a small civic grant project in Cobble Ford. The grant, which he facilitated, allowed the hamlet to repair a historic stone well cover that had become a safety hazard. The work is finished, and the well is now safely covered.

2.4 Coralie Greenshaw shared that she has created a simple glossary explaining common healthcare terms like 'co-pay' and 'referral' in plain language. It is a single laminated sheet. Three Quadling clinics are now keeping copies at their front desks. She noted that several patients have commented that it helps them understand their paperwork better.

2.5 Mott Peppercombe gave a brief report from the Brickway Works bridge crew. He stated that his crew recently used a quick-set concrete mix to fill and level a cracked concrete approach slab on a little-used farm track bridge near Bluebell Crossing. The work was done to prevent further deterioration from water ingress. The repair is holding.

2.6 Regarding Juniper Hazelby, Magnus Greendale mentioned that he and others had heard about her contribution to last year's Gillikin Light Festival. He said the word among liaisons was that Juniper provided the precise metal framework for a large kinetic sculpture that was a centerpiece of the event. Juniper Hazelby confirmed she had worked on the project but noted the framework was a subcontract from the main fabricator. She did not elaborate further.

3. Discussion: Improving Communication Between Offices and Residents
3.1 Magnus Greendale initiated a discussion on the persistent issue of public notices being written in overly formal language. He stated, "We get fewer complaints when the words are simpler. My recycling bin project proved that. But getting other departments to adopt the practice is slow."

3.2 Coralie Greenshaw agreed, relating it to her glossary work. "People shouldn't need a translator for basic services," she said.

3.3 Heath Gatecombe suggested that liaisons could compile examples of successful plain-language revisions from their respective areas to create a shared resource. Tomas Saffronley noted that such a resource would need approval from the central communications office to be used widely.

3.4 Juniper Hazelby asked Tomas to repeat the point about central office approval. After he did, she said, "Right. So we'd need a spec for that resource before we build it."

3.5 Action: Magnus Greendale and Coralie Greenshaw will draft two or three examples of revised public notices/forms for review at the next meeting.

4. Liaison Support Requests
4.1 Mott Peppercombe raised an issue about the standard forms for reporting minor bridge wear. He finds the current form has too many fields irrelevant to initial field assessment. "My crew spots a crack, they need to log the location and size, not write an essay on drainage patterns from five years ago. That comes later."

4.2 Tomas Saffronley said he would inquire about the possibility of a simplified 'field observation' version of the form. Heath Gatecombe offered to provide feedback from the ward perspective on what information is most critical for initial reporting.

4.3 Action: Tomas Saffronley will follow up with the Infrastructure Forms office and report back.

5. Any Other Business
5.1 Rowan Bell reminded the group of the Network's Summer Social on July 20th.

5.2 Juniper Hazelby asked if there was a standard process for liaisons to share technical specifications for public works projects across regions (e.g., bridge components, signage brackets). A brief discussion confirmed there is not a formal channel. Tomas Saffronley suggested this could be added to the agenda for a future meeting focused on inter-regional projects.

6. Next Meeting
Agreed for Wednesday, 10 July 2025, at 7:00 p.m. at the Emerald City Chamber meeting room.

Meeting adjourned at 8:30 p.m.
Minutes recorded by Rowan Bell.

experience_leads.summary: Pim Plumstead reported completing a prototype of an adapted knight's tabard with magnetic closures for a wheelchair-using actor, which was approved by the actor and stage manager.

evidence.quote: A prototype was completed last week and approved by the actor and the stage manager.
evidence.context:
Festival Committee
Meeting Minutes
Date: November 26, 2024
Present: Rowan Bell (Community Manager, Secretary), Pim Plumstead, Julian Park, Quill Tincombe, Mabry Rushcombe

1. Welcome and Updates
   Rowan Bell welcomed members and called the meeting to order at 6:05 PM at the Chamber Hall annex. The minutes from the October meeting were approved.

2. Project Reports
   2.1. Accessibility in Performance Costumes
   Pim Plumstead reported on adapting a knight's tabard for a wheelchair-using actor in the upcoming Brickway Players production. The standard side seams were replaced with a series of magnetic closures, allowing the actor to remove and replace the costume unaided during a standard 15-minute intermission. A prototype was completed last week and approved by the actor and the stage manager. Pim noted the magnets are sewn into a reinforced channel and covered with a matching fabric flap for safety and aesthetics.

   2.2. Puppet Repair Clinic
   Quill Tincombe summarized the free puppet repair clinic held on November 12 at the Lantern Row community center. He repaired seventeen puppets over four hours, with common issues being torn seams on felt animals and loose wooden dowel joints on marionettes. Quill mentioned one parent brought in a puppet that had been chewed by a family pet, which required a full replacement of the head's internal stuffing and a careful patch job. He used materials from his own workshop and said the event was 'a lovely bit of chaos, with children watching wide-eyed as their friends came back to life.'

3. New Proposals and Planned Work
   3.1. Modular Storage System
   Julian Park presented initial sketches for modular storage racks designed for the Committee's shared warehouse space. The concept involves interlocking wooden frames that can be configured to hold folded tents, tables of varying lengths, and rolled banners. Julian is planning to source reclaimed timber from the Timber Verge Repair Co-op and hopes to have a working prototype by mid-December for committee feedback. This is a planned project awaiting final measurements of the warehouse bay.

   3.2. Community Banner Workshop
   Mabry Rushcombe proposed a public workshop to create a large patchwork banner commemorating the Emerald City's founding anniversary. The plan is to invite residents to bring fabric scraps and contribute a stitched square under guidance. Mabry envisions the banner being completed over a series of weekend sessions in Gate Quarter early next year and displayed during the anniversary festivities. This is a planned initiative; Mabry will draft a materials list and potential venue options for the next meeting.

4. Logistics and Scheduling
   The next Festival Committee meeting is scheduled for December 17, 2024. Rowan Bell will check the availability of the Chamber Hall annex.
   Action Items:
   - Julian Park: Finalize warehouse measurements and produce a cost estimate for the modular storage prototype by Dec 10.
   - Mabry Rushcombe: Develop a draft schedule and material requirements for the banner workshop for review at the next meeting.
   - Rowan Bell: Circulate contact information for the Brickway Transit Union regarding potential transport of banner materials.

5. Other Business
   Pim mentioned that Spectacle Lane has a surplus of green velvet off-cuts from a recent project and offered them for the banner workshop. Mabry accepted the offer.
   Quill inquired about liability insurance for public repair clinics; Rowan agreed to look into the network's coverage.
   Meeting adjourned at 7:20 PM.

Respectfully submitted,
Rowan Bell
Community Manager, Emerald City Leadership Network

Attending: Rosa Clay, Pim Plumstead, Aurelia Ashmere, Toby Brickwick, Ansel Wickby. Rowan Bell (noting).

evidence.context:
Post-event debrief: Meadow Mutual Aid Network Check-In, November 2025.

Attended: Ezra Hedgebourne (Blue Orchard), Sable Orchardfield (Eastfield), Odile Pepperby (Lantern Row), Calla Copperby (Bluebell Crossing), Briony Oakmere (Gate Quarter). Rowan Bell present as facilitator.

General atmosphere was energetic and positive. A lot of cross-pollination of ideas between different regions and types of work (care, transport, food, goods). Focus was on sharing what's been done lately and what's being looked at, no formal decisions required.

Item 1: Updates from the field.
- Ezra reported on the new mending sessions at the Blue Orchard community center. He connected a retired seamstress who wanted to help with the network. They've set up a weekly two-hour slot. In the first month, they repaired about twenty items—clothes, torn curtains, a backpack. It's become a social spot; a few people stay just to chat even if they don't have mending. Ezra emphasized the 'we' of it: 'We're keeping skills in the community and saving people a trip to the tailor.'
- Odile gave a quiet, dry update from Lantern Row. She worked directly with the pharmacy on Brickway that serves the care home. They used to deliver prescriptions on three different days depending on the supplier, which was confusing for staff and sometimes led to delays. Odile got them to consolidate to one dedicated delivery day. 'Now the boxes arrive, I sign for them, and the residents get their medications on time. It's not glamorous, but it prevents a dozen small crises a month.'
- Calla was very direct about the produce run. She set up an arrangement with the Quadling farmers market to collect unsold but still fresh produce at closing time. The first run was last week. Meadow Mutual Aid volunteers with carts met the vendors, loaded up, and distributed the food to forty families in Bluebell Crossing and the southern Emerald City precincts that same evening. 'No storage, no fuss. Food moved from where it was surplus to where it was needed in about three hours.'
- Briony described the coat drive initiative. She got permission to place a clearly marked bin at the front of her tram on the Gate Quarter-to-Market Square route. For one week, she made announcements and kept an eye on it. She collected over thirty gently used coats. 'People would get on, see the bin, and sometimes get off at the next stop to go home and fetch a coat. It was very simple.' The coats have been passed to the Mutual Aid network for sorting and distribution.

Item 2: Ideas in progress.
- Sable mentioned that other members of Meadow Mutual Aid have been talking to her about an idea. She's heard from several parents in the network that there's interest in a toy and book lending library. The Eastfield Childcare Co-op has a storage shed that isn't fully used. Sable is looking into the feasibility—what it would take to clean it out, set up shelves, and create a simple check-out system. She was clear: 'We're just at the looking-into-it stage. I'm hearing the need, so we're seeing if the co-op space can be part of the solution.'

Item 3: Open discussion and cross-connections.
- Ezra asked Briony if the tram collection could be a recurring thing, maybe for blankets in the deep winter. Briony said she'd ask her supervisor but thinks a weekend drive might be easier to manage than a full week.
- Odile asked Calla if the produce distribution included areas near care homes, suggesting some residents on fixed incomes might benefit. Calla said the current route doesn't but they can adjust; she'll get the route list to Odile to see if any stops align.
- Sable's library idea got a lot of positive murmurs. Ezra offered to connect her with the retired seamstress, who he said has a lot of children's books she's been meaning to find a home for.

Item 4: Next steps and actions.
- Calla will share the produce distribution route with Odile by end of week. (Action: Calla)
- Briony will inquire about a weekend blanket drive on the trams and report back. (Action: Briony)
- Sable will draft a simple proposal for the shed library to share with the co-op board and the wider network for feedback. (Action: Sable)
- Rowan to circulate these notes and check in on actions in December.

No major logistical hurdles identified. The group agreed to check in again in the new year, possibly with a focus on winter preparedness projects.

To the Founders' Gala Nomination Committee,

I'm writing to nominate Ren Hazelham for recognition at this year's Gala, on behalf of the Emerald City Chamber. I'm Cecily Orchardham, over at the Emerald Gate Hotel. My reason is straightforward: Ren's work exemplifies the sort of quiet, daily excellence that holds a community together, and I think we should celebrate it.

My own recent experience gives me a fresh appreciation for it. Last month, during that flicker of a power outage in the Junction Quarter, our elevators were down. It was a minor scramble, but we had twelve guests needing to check out with luggage. We set up a manual log and stored everything securely in the lobby until power was restored. It was a simple, practical fix to keep things moving—the kind of thing we all do in our roles.

That's why Ren's project struck such a chord with me. I was in Hazelham Hardware a few weeks ago and noticed the plumbing section looked...unusually serene. Ren mentioned, in that dry way of his, that he'd spent a whole morning on it. He'd taken a single, chaotic bin of mixed washers and sorted them into a new drawer system, each compartment clearly labeled by millimeter diameter. No fanfare, no announcement. He just did it.

The result is that now, when a flustered homeowner comes in with a leaky tap, or a contractor needs fifty washers of a specific size, Ren—or any of his staff—can find exactly what's needed in seconds. That's more than tidiness. That's respect for other people's time and emergencies. It's a small act of order that ripples outward, making everyone's day a little smoother, a little less fraught.

In a network built on practical cooperation, Ren Hazelham's morning with the washers is a perfect model. It's the infrastructure of care, built one drawer at a time. I hope you'll agree he deserves the Chamber's nod.

Sincerely,
Cecily Orchardham
Manager, Emerald Gate Hotel

Rowan Bell · Community Manager · Timber Verge Repair Co-op debrief · June 2025

Post-meetup notes. Held at the South Meadow community hall. About fifteen attendees, a mix of co-op members and folks from the network's other circles who have an interest in woodwork, tools, or logistics.

Arthur Keene was there, of course, holding court by the tea urn. He didn't mention the dining table himself, but Hattie Tinstead brought it up. She said she’d heard from a neighbor in Quadling Country that Arthur had taken on a big old dining table missing its extension supports. The owner thought it was junk. Arthur apparently spent three days picking through scrap oak at the back of the Timber Verge yard, found pieces with the right grain, and hand-cut new supports so the leaf fits snug and doesn’t wobble. The neighbor is thrilled; says the table seats the whole family again. Arthur just nodded slowly and said, 'It’s all in the joint. A sliding dovetail, if you take your time, will outlast the tree it came from.' Then he launched into a story about a Gillikin cedar chest from sixty years ago.

Hattie Tinstead showed up with a canvas roll. She laid out a half-dozen pairs of fabric shears on the table. They were the ones from the Tinsmith Row community centre’s sewing group. She said last month the group was ready to throw them out, they were so dull they’d just chew fabric. She took them all, used a honing guide to get the angle right every time, and worked them on an oilstone. She demonstrated on one pair, cutting through a scrap of thick wool felt like it was butter. The shears are back in circulation. She mentioned she’s going to run a sharpening workshop at the tool library next quarter if there’s interest.

Talk of the tool library brought up Teo Brickholt’s name. A couple of people from the Brickway Transit Union said they’d heard Teo’s been instrumental in getting a neighborhood tool library started over in Green Market. He’s not just donating surplus hand tools—screwdrivers, wrenches, a couple of hand planes—from his hardware store, but he’s also been advising on the check-out system. He suggested a simple ledger and tags, something physical that doesn’t rely on everyone having a scroll-screen. They’re still in the planning stages, but they have a shelf unit and a donated lockbox now.

Dacey Barleybourne was in from Gillikin Falls. Gruff as ever, but had a good story. Said a delivery of rye came into the mill with higher moisture than usual. Could have sat and sweated, gone moldy in the silo. Instead of just processing it on the usual schedule, Dacey diverted the batch. Had the crew spread it all in the shallow storage bins overnight, cranked up the air circulation. Let it sit for a full day. They processed it the next morning, and the yield was fine. No must, no waste. Dacey said it was just paying attention. 'Grain tells you what it needs, if you listen.'

Abel Wickridge was the last to share. He drives freight out of Eastfield. Said there was a major snarl on the main Eastfield approach last Tuesday—a wagon lost a wheel, blocked both lanes. Dispatch was telling everyone to wait. Abel knew the schedule was tight for a load of milled timber headed to a framing crew in Emerald City. He remembered an old quarry road that cuts behind the hill. It’s rough, seldom-used, but passable if you take it slow. He took the detour, bumped along for forty minutes, and rejoined the Brickway past the blockage. Delivered the pallets only twenty minutes late. The foreman at the site didn’t even know there’d been a problem. Abel shrugged. 'Better a dusty truck than a missed deadline.'

Open actions from the meetup: Hattie will draft a date for the sharpening workshop and send it to the network calendar. A few folks asked if the tool library system Teo’s helping with could be a template for other neighborhoods; I’ll reach out to Teo to see if he’s willing to share notes. Arthur mentioned the co-op’s scrap pile is getting a bit too 'curated'—needs a proper sort-through. Dacey and Abel got talking about grain shipments and road conditions; might be a useful connection for the network’s logistics circle to follow up on.

Overall mood was focused and practical. Less about big ideas, more about the specific, tangible fixes people are doing in their own patches. Good energy.
